column5: unknown owner; restore the animal
column6: The verse anticipates finding a straying animal when its owner is not near or is not known, keeping it until the owner seeks it, and restoring it; this is a close legal counterpart to the dālla camel whose rab/mālik is unknown.

column5: straying ox or sheep
column6: The command to return a brother’s ox or sheep that has gone astray gives the commentary’s escaped animal a concrete action and owner relation rather than treating “straying” as an abstraction.

column5: enemy’s wandering ox or donkey
column6: Even an enemy’s wandering ox or donkey must be returned; the scene joins a loose pack animal to the obligation created by its known owner.

column5: when a roadside animal counts as lost
column6: The mishnah distinguishes an animal merely grazing on a road from one whose state shows genuine loss, then requires return; it gives a legal test for the commentary’s concrete dālla rather than equating every free animal with a lost one.

column5: identifying signs for restitution
column6: The discussion of simanim in the law of lost property makes an identifying sign the means by which an item can be restored; it is a direct legal analogue to the camel’s wasm/sīmah by which it is recognized.

column5: speckled and spotted flock as wages
column6: Jacob sets visibly marked sheep and goats apart as his wages, so an animal’s visible feature allocates it within a flock to a particular claimant.

column5: visible color proving ownership or theft
column6: Jacob says the flock’s visible coloring will demonstrate his innocence and expose a stolen animal; this makes an animal mark an evidentiary sign of whose it is.

column5: ox knows owner; donkey master’s manger
column6: Isaiah says an ox knows its owner and a donkey its master’s manger while Israel does not know; it directly parallels the commentary’s claim that livestock recognize owner and place while humans can be more lost.

column5: lost sheep; misleading shepherds; resting place
column6: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep, says their shepherds led them astray, and says they forgot their resting place; it combines the commentary’s stray animal, failed leader, path, and merabb-like place of remaining.

column5: lost sheep asks to be sought
column6: The speaker says that he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asks the Lord to seek his servant, turning the lost-animal image into a prayer for recovery by the rightful master.

column5: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
column6: God’s shepherding promise explicitly seeks the lost and returns the strayed, supplying the caring owner-side of the commentary’s camel left in an unowned place.

column5: Moses follows a runaway lamb to water
column6: The midrash has Moses pursue a lamb that has run from Jethro’s flock, find it drinking, and carry it back; God makes that care the reason he can shepherd Israel, joining the stray animal, water/pasture, and qualified leader.

column5: one lost sheep sought by its owner
column6: The man who loses one of a hundred sheep goes after the lost one, a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s animal separated from its owner and herd.

column5: one strayed sheep valued above the ninety-nine
column6: This lost-sheep version has the shepherd seek the one that strayed and value it above the ninety-nine, a distinct Christian apocryphal intensification of the individual animal’s recovery.

column5: straying sheep return to Shepherd and Overseer
column6: The addressees were sheep going astray but have returned to a Shepherd and Overseer; it connects wandering from the way with restoration to a guiding, responsible figure.

column5: own sheep called by name and led out
column6: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining recognized belonging with a leader who initiates the flock’s movement.

column5: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
column6: The shepherd goes in front and the sheep follow his voice, the closest New Testament rendering of the commentary’s front animal/hādī followed by the rest of the herd.

column5: owner and flock know one another
column6: The reciprocal knowledge of shepherd and sheep gives a direct positive counterpart to the dālla whose rab and mālik cannot be identified.

column5: sheep without a shepherd
column6: Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image makes the lack of a leading, responsible figure the cause of a dispersed and distressed flock.

column5: leader goes out before the people
column6: Moses asks for a leader who will go out before and bring the people in, so that they will not be sheep without a shepherd; it applies the commentary’s front-leading herd image to communal guidance.

column5: God goes before to lead by the way
column6: The Lord goes before Israel in the pillar to lead them on the way, giving the request for guidance a concrete leading-before movement like the commentary’s hādī.

column5: what goes ahead seeks a resting place
column6: The ark goes before the people to seek out a resting place for them; it binds the front guide to finding the place where the moving community may remain.

column5: people led like sheep through wilderness
column6: God leads the people out like sheep and guides them like a flock in the wilderness, directly joining flock, guidance, and a journey through exposed country.

column5: YHWH as shepherd
column6: The declaration that the Lord is the speaker’s shepherd gives the commentary’s rab/mālik relation its classic pastoral form: a flock has a guiding provider.

column5: green pastures and resting waters
column6: The shepherd makes the sheep lie in green pastures and leads them to resting waters, closely matching the herd’s fixed place and the pasture it finds pleasing.

column5: leading in right tracks
column6: The shepherd restores life and leads in right tracks, providing a pastoral analogue to ihdinā and the straight path rather than guidance as a disembodied instruction.

column5: shepherd feeds, gathers, and gently leads
column6: The divine shepherd feeds the flock, gathers lambs, and gently leads nursing ewes; it develops both pasture-care and differentiated leadership within a herd.

column5: good pasture and secure lying down
column6: God promises good pasture where the flock will lie down, a precise counterpart to the merabb where camels stay and the land whose grazing is approved.

column5: Wisdom guides on straight paths
column6: Wisdom guides the righteous person on straight paths in its account of divine guidance; it supplies a Jewish Second Temple formulation for the commentary’s moving sense of the straight path.

column5: unknown paths made straight
column6: God leads the blind on an unknown way and makes crooked ground straight, directly pairing guidance with the contrast between a right path and a deviating one.

column5: perverting the straight paths of the Lord
column6: The rebuke names the straight paths of the Lord and accuses its target of making them crooked, a concrete New Testament counterpart to the commentary’s path that turns aside from the qasd.

column5: forsaking the straight way and going astray
column6: The text says its opponents abandoned the straight way and went astray, retaining both sides of the commentary’s road vocabulary rather than merely a general moral failure.

column5: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
column6: The Lamb becomes the flock’s shepherd and guides them to springs of water; this striking reversal makes an animal the leader while retaining the commentary’s guide-and-pasture movement.

column5: followers go wherever the Lamb goes
column6: The redeemed follow the Lamb wherever he goes, an explicit following relation that gives the commentary’s herd behind its leading animal a Christian eschatological form.

column5: all cattle belong to God
column6: God declares every forest beast and the cattle on a thousand hills to be his, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary’s claim that every creature has its rab/mālik.

column5: divine blessing includes six thousand camels
column6: The verse calls Job’s latter state blessed and immediately counts his camels among its abundance, closely matching the commentary’s association of camels with niʿma, benefit, and blessing.

column5: camels bear precious cargo over distance
column6: A multitude of camels carries gold and frankincense and brings proclamation of the Lord’s praises; it closely matches the commentary’s load-bearing animals and its hamd/benefit frame.

column5: grass grown for cattle
column6: God causes grass to grow for cattle, giving the good pasture in the commentary a providential source rather than treating it as only a herd preference.

column5: donkey lying under its burden
column6: The command to help an enemy’s donkey collapsed under its load gives an ethical counterpart to the commentary’s carrying mount: its legs bear burdens, so the human associated with it must assist.

column5: human rule over living creatures
column6: Humanity is told to rule the moving creatures, a creation-account counterpart to the commentary’s Qur’anic picture of livestock made subject to human possession; the biblical verse frames that relation as a commission.

column5: the righteous know an animal’s needs
column6: The righteous person knows the life or needs of his animal, adding responsibility and attention to the commentary’s owner-and-herd relation.

column5: divine pity includes much cattle
column6: God’s stated pity for Nineveh explicitly includes its many cattle, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary’s move from useful animals to the Lord’s compassion.

column5: wild ass sent free and unbound
column6: Job asks who released the wild ass and loosed its bonds; it gives the commentary’s wild-ass herd a theological counterweight to the tame, owner-marked animal.

column5: wild ass given wilderness as home
column6: God gives the wild ass the steppe and salt land as its dwelling, making the wilderness place in the commentary’s lost-animal definition a positive habitat for a creature not domesticated by humans.

column5: horse and mule need bit and bridle
column6: The psalm contrasts a human who should understand with horse and mule controlled by bridle; its training image usefully complicates the commentary’s tame camel and animal-led guidance without making the two moral claims identical.

column5: name written on the forehead
column6: The Lamb’s followers visibly bear his and his Father’s name on their foreheads, a personal and covenantal analogue to the commentary’s visible brand that makes an animal’s belonging recognizable.

column5: bees ordered under a king
column6: Basil’s bee discussion presents the hive as an ordered community under a king; it supplies a Christian natural-theological analogue to the commentary’s malik of the bees, though section divisions vary by edition.

column5: unmuzzled ox re-read for human workers
column6: Paul invokes the rule against muzzling a grain-treading ox in an argument about the support of human workers; this Christian reading turns a working animal’s claim into a claim about labor, relevant to the commentary’s tamed, load-bearing animal.

column5: Hebrew melek goes before the people
column6: Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary’s m-l-k label, and this verse asks for a king who will go before Israel; its own context thus pairs the cognate title with the front-leading function the commentary gives to milk.

column5: Hebrew ʿbd, serving YHWH
column6: Hebrew ʿbd is cognate with the commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d label; Joshua’s choice to serve the Lord supplies the worship-side use of that family, without transferring the camel-treatment sense into the verse.

column5: Hebrew noʿam and paths
column6: Hebrew noʿam is cognate with the commentary’s n-ʿ-m label, and Wisdom’s ways are called ways of pleasantness; the verse joins the source’s blessing/pleasant-pasture association to a path.

column5: Aramaic Rabbi as an authority title
column6: The source labels rabb as an owner-title; John retains the Semitic title Rabbi and glosses it as Teacher. The likely cognate relation supplies only a title comparison here, not evidence that John’s teacher image is a flock-owner image.
